U.S. container imports hit a record high in September, up 10.3% from a year earlier to 2.55 million twenty-foot equivalent units, according to Descartes . The company released the findings Oct. 8 in its latest Global Shipping Report.
What’s Related
Imports fell 2.2% from August but were 24.8% above September 2019. Through the first nine months of 2026, total imports were up 0.8% from the same period last year, marking the first time this year that cumulative volume moved ahead of 2025.
Shipments from China were a major part of September’s increase, rising 21.2% from a year earlier. China accounted for 36.3% of all U.S. container imports, compared with 34% in August.
The results also showed a shift toward West Coast ports and longer transit delays at most major ports. Imports from the 10 largest countries of origin were essentially unchanged from August, as gains from China, India, and Taiwan offset declines elsewhere.
China shipments on the rise
U.S. imports from China totaled 924,454 twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, up 4.5% from August. TEUs are a standard measure of container volume based on a 20-foot container.
Plastics led China-origin imports, followed by furniture and bedding, and toys and sporting goods. Those three categories accounted for approximately 38% of September’s container volume from China.
Seven of the top 10 countries supplying U.S. container imports recorded monthly declines. China’s increase largely offset those losses, leaving the group’s overall volume nearly flat.
West Coast ports gain ground
Los Angeles imports rose 8.8% from August, while Long Beach gained 5.9%. Oakland increased 14.4%, and Tacoma rose 7%.
Other major ports recorded declines, including Houston at 16.5%, Norfolk at 13.4%, Charleston at 10.3% and Savannah at 9.6%. Gulf Coast imports overall fell 14.8% to 215,324 TEUs, below their rolling 12-month average.
The five leading West Coast ports handled 46.7% of U.S. container imports in September. The five leading East and Gulf Coast ports handled 39.7% of U.S. container imports in September.
Increased delays at most major ports
Descartes’ transit-delay measure increased at eight of the 10 major ports. New York/New Jersey recorded the largest increase, rising 1.5 days to 8.3 days, while Houston rose 1.4 days to 7.2 days.
The measure compares the initial estimated arrival date on a shipment’s bill of lading with the date Descartes receives the customs-processed shipping record. It should not be read as the number of days a container sits at a terminal.
